title: Body and Health
tagline: Sleep, eat, move, and know what to do when things go wrong.
description: Build the everyday habits that keep you healthy: enough sleep, food that fuels you, a simple strength and cardio routine, and regular checkups. Then learn how to handle stress, when and how to get help for your mental health, and the first aid basics for emergencies. The first aid lessons are an introduction, not a replacement for a certified class.

units.title: Sleep, Screens and Self-Care
units.description: Get the sleep you need, protect your eyes and back, and keep up with hygiene and checkups.

levels.title: Sleep That Works
levels.summary: How much sleep you need, what happens when you skip it, and habits that help.

steps.title: How much do you need?
steps.body:
The CDC recommends:
- **Teens (13-17)**: 8-10 hours a night
- **Adults (18-60)**: 7 or more hours a night

Sleep is when your body repairs muscle, your brain stores what you learned, and your immune system recharges. Short sleep is linked to worse grades and reaction time, more colds, more snacking, low mood, and drowsy driving crashes.

> You can't train yourself to need less sleep. You just get used to feeling tired.
steps.tip: Set a bedtime alarm, not just a wake-up alarm. Count back 8-9 hours from when you have to get up, and have your phone remind you 30 minutes before that.

steps.prompt: You fall asleep at 11:30 p.m. and your alarm goes off at 6:30 a.m. How many hours of sleep do you get?
steps.explain:
11:30 p.m. to 12:30 a.m. is 1 hour.

12:30 a.m. to 6:30 a.m. is 6 more hours.

Total: **7 hours**. That meets the adult minimum but is 1-3 hours short of what a 13-17-year-old needs.
steps.hint: Count in two parts: from 11:30 p.m. to 12:30 a.m., then from 12:30 a.m. to 6:30 a.m.

steps.prompt: A 16-year-old needs about 9 hours of sleep but gets 6 on school nights and feels wiped out. What's the best fix?
options: Move bedtime earlier, 15-30 minutes at a time, until they're closer to 9 hours
Sleep until noon every Saturday to catch up
Drink coffee every morning to push through
Nothing. Teens adjust to 6 hours after a few weeks
feedback: Right. Small, steady changes to bedtime fix the cause.
Big sleep-ins shift your body clock and make Sunday night harder.
Caffeine covers up tiredness but doesn't repay the sleep, and it can make nights worse.
You get used to feeling tired. You don't stop needing the sleep.
steps.hint: Which choice fixes the cause instead of covering up the tiredness?
steps.explain: Missing 3 hours a night for 5 nights is 15 hours, almost two full nights of sleep. Shifting bedtime earlier in small steps is the change most likely to stick.

steps.title: Habits that help
steps.body:
- **Same schedule every day**, weekends included, as much as possible.
- **Screens off at least 30 minutes before bed.** Phones keep your brain alert.
- **Cool, dark, quiet room.**
- **No caffeine in the afternoon or evening**, including energy drinks and many sodas.
- **No big meals right before bed.**
- **Get daylight and exercise** during the day.

If you can't fall asleep after a while, get up and do something calm in dim light, then try again.
steps.tip: Tonight, charge your phone across the room instead of next to your bed. You'll scroll less, and you'll have to get up to turn off the alarm.

steps.prompt: Which habits help you fall asleep and stay asleep? Select all that apply.
options: Waking up at the same time on weekends as on weekdays
Scrolling videos in bed until you feel sleepy
Keeping your room cool and dark
An energy drink at 5 p.m. to finish homework
Getting outside during the day
steps.explain: A steady schedule, a cool dark room and daylight help set your body clock. Late screens and late caffeine push sleep later and make it lighter.

steps.prompt: It's 11 p.m. You're exhausted and need to drive 25 minutes home from a friend's house. You keep yawning and your eyes feel heavy. What's the best choice?

options.text: Don't drive. Ask to stay over, get a ride, or call a parent.
options.feedback: Right. Drowsy driving slows reaction time a lot like drunk driving does.

options.text: Roll the windows down and blast music so you stay awake.
options.feedback: These tricks don't work for long. You can nod off for a few seconds without realizing it.

options.text: Drink a coffee and leave right away.
options.feedback: Caffeine takes time to kick in and doesn't replace sleep.

steps.explain: If you're nodding off, the only real fix is sleep. Plan a backup ride before late nights.
steps.hint: Which option actually removes the danger, instead of just making you feel more awake for a few minutes?

steps.prompt: Sleeping in until noon on Saturday fully cancels out a week of short nights.
steps.explain: Catch-up sleep helps a bit, but it also shifts your body clock, making Sunday night harder. A steady schedule works better.

steps.prompt: Put a wind-down routine for a 10:30 p.m. bedtime in order.
items: Finish caffeine by early afternoon
Eat dinner a few hours before bed
Put your phone on the charger outside the bed by 10:00
Do something calm: shower, read, stretch
Lights out at 10:30
steps.explain: Each step lowers alertness. Charging the phone away from your bed removes the biggest temptation.
steps.hint: Start with what happens earliest in the day and end with lights out.

steps.prompt: What time do you need to wake up on school or work days? Work back to the bedtime that gives you enough sleep, and name one habit you'll change to hit it.
steps.placeholder: Wake at ___, so bed by ___. Habit to change: ___

levels.title: Screens, Eyes and Posture
levels.summary: Eye strain, the 20-20-20 rule and a desk setup that saves your neck and back.

steps.title: Tired eyes
steps.body:
When you stare at a screen, you blink less, so your eyes dry out and feel tired. Common signs: dry or burning eyes, blurry vision, headaches.

The American Academy of Ophthalmology suggests the **20-20-20 rule**:

> Every **20 minutes**, look at something about **20 feet** away for **20 seconds**.

Also: keep the screen about an arm's length away, slightly below eye level, and reduce glare. If symptoms continue, get an eye exam; you may need glasses.

source.label: AAO: Computers, digital devices and eye strain

steps.tip: Next time you study on a screen, set a repeating 20-minute timer. When it rings, look out a window or across the room for 20 seconds.

steps.prompt: Match each part of the 20-20-20 rule to its number.
pairs: How often to take an eye break
steps.explain: Looking far away relaxes the focusing muscles in your eyes. Set a timer until it becomes a habit.

steps.prompt: You'll study on a laptop for 2 hours. What's the easiest way to follow the 20-20-20 rule?
options: Set a repeating 20-minute timer and look at something far away for 20 seconds each time
Take one long break when the 2 hours are done
Turn the screen brightness all the way up
Close your eyes for 20 minutes every hour
feedback: Right. A timer makes it automatic: about 6 short breaks in 2 hours.
One break at the end leaves your eyes working up close for 2 hours straight.
Very bright screens add glare and can make strain worse.
That's not the rule, and it would eat most of your study time.
steps.hint: The rule has three parts: how often, how far away, and for how long.
steps.explain: Every 20 minutes, look about 20 feet away for 20 seconds. Looking far away relaxes the eye muscles that focus up close.

steps.title: Text neck and desk setup
steps.body:
Looking down at a phone for hours loads your neck. Slouching at a desk strains your back and shoulders.

A simple setup:
- **Screen** top at or slightly below eye level (stack books under a laptop and use a separate keyboard if you can).
- **Feet** flat on the floor, knees about level with hips.
- **Back** supported, shoulders relaxed, elbows near 90 degrees.
- **Phone** raised toward eye level instead of dropping your head.

The best posture is your *next* one: stand up and move every 30-60 minutes.
steps.tip: Stack a few books under your laptop so the top of the screen is near eye level. Add a cheap separate keyboard so your arms can stay low.

steps.prompt: Which changes would help someone with neck pain from long gaming sessions? Select all that apply.
options: Raise the monitor so the top is near eye level
Take a short movement break every 30-60 minutes
Lean closer to the screen to see better
Keep feet flat and back supported
Play lying on your stomach with your head propped up
steps.explain: Screen height, support and regular movement reduce strain. Leaning in and propping your head up both bend the neck forward.
steps.hint: Look for changes that bring the screen up to you instead of bending your neck down to it.

steps.prompt: You've had headaches and blurry vision after every school day for two weeks, even though you take screen breaks. What should you do?

options.text: Book an eye exam with an optometrist or ophthalmologist.
options.feedback: Yes. Ongoing symptoms despite good habits are a reason to get checked; you may need glasses.

options.text: Buy blue-light glasses online and skip the exam.
options.feedback: Eye doctors say there isn't good evidence blue-light glasses prevent eye strain, and you'd miss a real vision problem.

options.text: Ignore it; everyone's eyes get tired.
options.feedback: Two weeks of headaches and blurry vision deserves a check.

steps.explain: Uncorrected vision problems are a common cause of headaches. An eye exam is quick and often covered by insurance.
steps.hint: Good habits didn't fix it. Who can actually check your vision?

steps.prompt: Staring at screens makes most people blink less often, which can dry out the eyes.
steps.explain: Concentrating on a screen lowers your blink rate. Breaks and conscious blinking help.

steps.title: Key takeaways
steps.body:
- Every 20 minutes, look 20 feet away for 20 seconds.
- Screen top at or a bit below eye level, an arm's length away.
- Feet flat, back supported, shoulders relaxed.
- Move every 30-60 minutes.
- Get an eye exam if headaches or blurry vision keep coming back.

levels.title: Hygiene and Checkups
levels.summary: Handwashing, teeth, skin, and which doctor visits to keep up with.

steps.title: Clean hands, fewer sick days
steps.body:
Handwashing is one of the best ways to avoid getting sick and spreading germs. The CDC says to scrub with soap for **at least 20 seconds**, about two rounds of "Happy Birthday."

Wash especially:
- before, during and after preparing food, and before eating
- after using the toilet
- after blowing your nose, coughing or sneezing
- after touching animals, pet food or trash
- before and after treating a cut or caring for someone sick

No sink? Hand sanitizer with at least 60% alcohol is the backup.
steps.tip: Keep a small bottle of hand sanitizer with at least 60% alcohol in your backpack or car for times when there's no sink.

steps.prompt: Put handwashing in order.
items: Wet your hands with clean running water
Apply soap and lather backs, between fingers and under nails
Scrub for at least 20 seconds
Rinse well under running water
Dry with a clean towel or air dryer
steps.explain: The scrubbing and lathering do the work; rinsing carries the germs away, and drying keeps hands from picking up new ones.

steps.title: Teeth, skin and body
steps.body:
- **Teeth**: brush twice a day with fluoride toothpaste and clean between teeth once a day (floss or picks). The American Dental Association recommends both.
- **Shower** regularly, and always after sweaty workouts. Use deodorant or antiperspirant daily.
- **Skin**: wash your face gently; don't pick at acne. Use broad-spectrum sunscreen, SPF 30 or higher, when outdoors.
- **Laundry**: workout clothes and towels go in the wash after each use; sheets about weekly.
steps.tip: Set a repeating phone reminder to replace your toothbrush every 3-4 months, or sooner if the bristles look frayed.

steps.prompt: Which are good daily or weekly habits? Select all that apply.
options: Brushing twice a day and cleaning between teeth daily
Rewearing sweaty gym clothes for a week
Washing hands before eating
Sunscreen for a day at the beach
Sharing a razor with a friend
steps.explain: Brushing and flossing, handwashing and sunscreen protect you. Sweaty clothes breed bacteria, and sharing razors can spread infections.

steps.title: Checkups to keep
steps.body:
- **Primary care doctor**: a regular physical, plus visits when something feels off. Find one *before* you're sick.
- **Dentist**: cleanings and checkups, usually once or twice a year, as your dentist advises.
- **Eye exam**: if you have glasses or contacts, or notice vision changes.
- **Vaccines**: a flu shot every year, plus others your doctor recommends.

Bring a list of questions and any medicines you take. Doctors keep your information private; be honest so they can actually help.
steps.tip: Look up an in-network primary care doctor on your insurance website and save the office number in your phone, even if you feel fine.

steps.prompt: Match the health need to who handles it.
pairs: Stubborn acne or a changing mole
steps.explain: Your primary care doctor is the home base and can refer you to specialists when needed.

steps.prompt: You just moved out and haven't seen a doctor in three years. You feel fine. What's the best move?

options.text: Find an in-network primary care doctor and book a checkup now, while you're healthy.
options.feedback: Exactly. A baseline visit catches problems early and gives you a doctor to call later.

options.text: Wait until you get sick, then go to the emergency room.
options.feedback: ERs are for emergencies and cost far more. Prevention is cheaper.

options.text: Skip doctors as long as you feel fine.
options.feedback: Many problems, like high blood pressure, have no symptoms early.

steps.explain: Most insurance plans cover a yearly preventive checkup at no cost to you when you use an in-network doctor.

steps.prompt: Rinsing your hands under water for five seconds without soap is about as good as a 20-second scrub with soap.
steps.explain: Soap plus scrubbing time is what lifts germs and grime off your skin. A quick rinse leaves most of them behind.

steps.prompt: When was your last physical, dental cleaning and eye exam? Write down which one you'll schedule next and when.
steps.placeholder: Physical: ___ Dentist: ___ Eyes: ___. Next I'll book ___ by ___.

units.title: Food and Water
units.description: Build balanced meals, read nutrition labels and stay hydrated.

levels.title: Building a Better Plate
levels.summary: Protein, fiber and whole foods, and why highly processed food is worth limiting.

steps.title: The big ideas
steps.body:
The **Dietary Guidelines for Americans, 2025-2030**, released in January 2026, focus on:
- **Whole, minimally processed foods**: vegetables, fruits, beans, whole grains, eggs, meat, fish, dairy, nuts.
- **Enough protein** at each meal.
- **Limiting highly processed foods**, added sugars and sugary drinks.

A simple plate: half vegetables and fruit, a quarter protein, a quarter whole grains or starchy foods, plus water.
steps.tip: At your next meal, look at your plate. If it isn't about half vegetables or fruit, add a handful of frozen vegetables or a piece of fruit.

steps.title: Protein at every meal
steps.body:
**Protein** builds and repairs muscle and keeps you full longer.

The 2025-2030 guidelines suggest more protein than older advice did (1.2-1.6 grams per kilogram of body weight a day). Some experts think that's more than most people need. But they agree on the simple part:

> Have a protein food at every meal.

Cheap protein foods: eggs, beans and lentils, Greek yogurt, milk, peanut butter, canned tuna, chicken thighs.
steps.tip: Add one protein food to the meal you usually skimp on, often breakfast: eggs, Greek yogurt, peanut butter on toast, or last night's leftover chicken.

steps.prompt: Your lunch is rice and vegetables. Which add-on gives it the most protein?
options: A scoop of black beans or a chicken thigh
A bigger scoop of rice
A glass of orange juice
A handful of chips
feedback: Right. Beans and chicken are both solid protein foods.
More rice adds energy but little protein.
Juice is mostly sugar and water.
Chips add salt and fat, not much protein.
steps.hint: Check the list of cheap protein foods from the last step.
steps.explain: Adding a protein food turns a side dish into a filling meal. Beans bring fiber too, which makes them one of the cheapest upgrades you can make.

steps.title: Fiber fills you up
steps.body:
**Fiber** is the part of plant foods your body can't fully digest. It keeps digestion regular, keeps you full, and is good for your heart.

Where to find it: beans, lentils, oats, whole grains, vegetables, fruit, nuts.

Most Americans eat far less fiber than recommended. You don't need to count grams. Just add one high-fiber food to each meal.
steps.tip: Swap one food this week for a high-fiber one: oatmeal instead of sugary cereal, or a can of rinsed beans stirred into soup, chili or rice.

steps.prompt: Most Americans already eat plenty of fiber, so there's no need to add more.
steps.explain: Most people get far less than the common target of about 14 grams per 1,000 calories (around 28 grams on a 2,000-calorie day). Beans, oats and fruit are easy ways to close the gap.

steps.prompt: Match each food to what it's especially rich in.
steps.explain: Most whole foods bring several nutrients at once. Beans are a cheap source of both fiber and protein.

steps.prompt: Which breakfast best fits the guidelines?
options: A frosted toaster pastry and a soda
Scrambled eggs, whole-grain toast and an orange
A large sweetened coffee drink
Skipping breakfast and grabbing chips at 10 a.m.
steps.explain: Eggs give protein, whole-grain toast and fruit give fiber, and none of it is highly processed. The others are mostly added sugar or skip real food.

steps.prompt: You're on a tight budget and want more protein and fiber. Which grocery plan works best?

options.text: Dried or canned beans, eggs, oats, frozen vegetables and a bag of chicken thighs.
options.feedback: Great. These are cheap, filling, long-lasting whole foods.

options.text: Protein bars and protein shakes for every meal.
options.feedback: Convenient sometimes, but expensive, highly processed and low in fiber.

options.text: Instant noodles because they're the cheapest.
options.feedback: Cheap per pack, but low in protein and fiber, and very high in sodium.

steps.explain: Frozen vegetables and canned beans are as nutritious as fresh and won't spoil before you use them.
steps.hint: Look for foods that are cheap, filling and keep for a while without spoiling.

steps.prompt: Frozen vegetables are usually much less nutritious than fresh ones.
steps.explain: Frozen vegetables are picked and frozen quickly, so they keep most of their nutrients. They're a cheap, low-waste option.

steps.title: Key takeaways
steps.body:
- Build meals from whole, minimally processed foods.
- Have a protein food at every meal.
- Add a high-fiber food to each meal; most people need more.
- Limit highly processed foods, added sugar and sugary drinks.
- Beans, eggs, oats and frozen vegetables are cheap wins.

levels.title: Reading Nutrition Labels
levels.summary: Serving sizes, percent Daily Value and spotting added sugar and sodium.

steps.title: Start with the serving
steps.body:
Every number on a Nutrition Facts label is for **one serving**, not the whole package.

1. Check **servings per container** and **serving size**.
2. Compare that to how much you'll actually eat.
3. Multiply.

A bag of chips with 2.5 servings means eating the whole bag is 2.5 times every number on the label.
steps.tip: Grab one snack you eat often and find its servings per container. Then be honest: how many servings do you really eat in one sitting?

steps.prompt: A can of soup lists 700 mg of sodium per serving and 2 servings per can. You eat the whole can. How much sodium do you get?
steps.hint: The label numbers are for one serving. How many servings are you eating?
steps.explain:
700 mg x 2 servings = **1,400 mg**.

The Daily Value for sodium is 2,300 mg, so one can of soup gives you more than half a day's sodium. Look for "low sodium" versions.

steps.title: The 5/20 rule
steps.body:
**% Daily Value (%DV)** shows how much one serving contributes to a day's worth of a nutrient. The FDA's quick guide:

> **5% DV or less** is low. **20% DV or more** is high.

Look for **high** fiber, vitamin D, calcium, iron and potassium. Look for **low** saturated fat, sodium and added sugars.

Key Daily Values: added sugars **50 g**, sodium **2,300 mg**.

source.label: FDA: Lows and highs of percent Daily Value

steps.tip: In the store, compare two versions of something you buy, like two cereals or two soups. Pick the one with the lower %DV for added sugars and sodium.

steps.prompt: A yogurt label shows **20% DV** for added sugars per serving. Using the 5/20 rule, how much added sugar is that?
options: High
Low
Medium, nothing to notice
You can't tell without knowing the grams
steps.hint: 5% DV or less is low. 20% DV or more is high.
steps.explain: 20% DV or more is high, so this yogurt is high in added sugar for one cup. Plain yogurt with fresh fruit is a lower-sugar swap.

steps.prompt: A bag of chips has 3 servings, and each serving is 10% DV for sodium. If you eat the whole bag, you get 10% DV of sodium.
steps.hint: Are the label numbers for the whole bag or for one serving?
steps.explain: Every number on the label is per serving. The whole bag is 3 servings: 3 x 10% = 30% DV, nearly a third of a day's sodium in one snack.

steps.prompt: Match each label item to whether you generally want it high or low.
pairs: Compare to what you'll actually eat
Shows ingredients from most to least by weight
steps.explain: Read fiber and added sugars first, then check the serving size and the first few ingredients.

steps.prompt: Two cereals: A has 12% DV fiber and 4% DV added sugars. B has 3% DV fiber and 24% DV added sugars. Which is the better everyday pick?
options: Cereal A
Cereal B
They're the same
You can't tell without the price
steps.explain: A is low in added sugar (under 5%) with more fiber. B is high in added sugar (over 20%) and low in fiber.
steps.hint: Use the 5/20 rule: you want fiber high and added sugars low.

steps.prompt: On an ingredients list, the first ingredient is the one there's the most of by weight.
steps.explain: Ingredients are listed from most to least by weight. If sugar or syrup is near the top, it's a sugary product.

steps.title: Key takeaways
steps.body:
- All label numbers are per serving; multiply for what you eat.
- 5% DV or less is low; 20% DV or more is high.
- Want high: fiber, vitamin D, calcium, iron, potassium.
- Want low: saturated fat, sodium, added sugars.
- Ingredients are listed most to least by weight.

levels.title: Drinks, Hydration and Caffeine
levels.summary: How much to drink, sugary drinks, and what caffeine and energy drinks do.

steps.title: Water first
steps.body:
Your body needs water to control temperature, move nutrients and keep your brain working. How much you need depends on your size, activity, and the weather. You need more in heat, during exercise, and when sick with fever, vomiting or diarrhea.

Simple checks:
- Drink with every meal and during exercise.
- Carry a reusable bottle.
- **Pale yellow urine** usually means you're well hydrated; dark yellow means drink more.

Food counts too: fruits, vegetables and soups contain lots of water.
steps.tip: Fill a reusable water bottle in the morning and keep it in sight, on your desk or in your bag. You drink more when it's always there.

steps.prompt: You want to drink 72 ounces of water a day. Your bottle holds 24 ounces. How many full bottles is that?
steps.explain: 72 / 24 = **3 bottles**. Tie them to your day: one by lunch, one by the end of school or work, one by dinner.
steps.hint: How many 24-ounce bottles fit into 72 ounces? Divide.

steps.title: Sugary drinks
steps.body:
**Sugary drinks** (soda, sweet tea, fruit drinks, sports drinks, energy drinks, sweet coffee drinks) are the biggest source of added sugar for many people. Their calories don't fill you up the way food does.

A single 20-ounce soda can have more added sugar than the Daily Value for a whole day (50 grams).

**Sports drinks** are made for long, sweaty exercise. For everyday activity, water is enough.
steps.tip: For one week, swap one sugary drink a day for water, sparkling water or unsweetened tea. Keep track of the money you don't spend.

steps.prompt: A 20-ounce soda has 65 grams of added sugar. The Daily Value for added sugars is 50 grams. What does that tell you?
options: One bottle is more than a whole day's worth of added sugar
One bottle is about a quarter of a day's added sugar
Soda sugar doesn't count as added sugar
It's fine as long as you drink it with a meal
feedback: Right. 65 grams is more than the 50-gram Daily Value.
65 grams is more than 50, not a quarter of it.
Sugar put into a drink is exactly what 'added sugar' means.
Drinking it with food doesn't change the amount of sugar.
steps.hint: Compare 65 with 50. Which is bigger?
steps.explain: 65 grams is about 130% of the Daily Value in one bottle. Swapping one soda a day for water removes a whole day's worth of added sugar.

steps.prompt: Which are signs you may need more fluids? Select all that apply.
options: Dark yellow urine
Headache and feeling dizzy on a hot day
Pale yellow urine
Very dry mouth after a long practice
Feeling fine after drinking water with each meal
steps.explain: Dark urine, dizziness, headache and dry mouth can all signal dehydration. Pale yellow urine is a good sign.

steps.title: Caffeine and energy drinks
steps.body:
**Caffeine** is in coffee, tea, many sodas and energy drinks. The FDA says up to about **400 mg a day** is generally fine for healthy adults, roughly two to three 12-ounce cups of coffee.

**Teens** should have much less, and medical experts advise teens to **avoid energy drinks**.

Too much caffeine causes jitters, a racing heart, anxiety and poor sleep. It stays in your body for hours, so an afternoon drink can still keep you up at night.

source.label: FDA: How much caffeine is too much?

steps.tip: Pick a caffeine cutoff time, like 2 p.m., and stick to it for a week. Notice whether you fall asleep faster.

steps.prompt: It's finals week. You're 17 and planning to drink two energy drinks a night to stay up studying. What's the better plan?

options.text: Skip the energy drinks, study in focused blocks earlier in the day, and protect your sleep so your brain stores what you learned.
options.feedback: Yes. Sleep is when memories get locked in, and teens are advised to avoid energy drinks.

options.text: Go ahead; caffeine has no side effects.
options.feedback: High doses can cause a racing heart, anxiety and insomnia, and can be dangerous for some people.

options.text: Pull an all-nighter the night before each exam.
options.feedback: Skipping sleep hurts memory and focus on test day.

steps.explain: Spaced studying plus real sleep beats cramming on caffeine.
steps.hint: What does your brain need in order to store what you studied?

steps.prompt: Match each drink to the best description.
pairs: Zero calories; the default for everyday thirst
Lots of added sugar, no nutrients
High caffeine; not advised for teens
steps.explain: Unflavored milk and unsweetened tea or coffee are also fine for adults. Save sugary drinks for occasional treats.

steps.title: Key takeaways
steps.body:
- Water first: drink with meals and during exercise.
- Pale yellow urine usually means you're hydrated.
- One soda can exceed a day's added sugar.
- Adults: up to about 400 mg caffeine a day. Teens: much less, and no energy drinks.
- Sports drinks are for long, sweaty workouts.

units.title: Move and Mind
units.description: Strength and cardio basics, a beginner routine that grows with you, and handling stress.

levels.title: How Much Exercise?
levels.summary: The activity guidelines for teens and adults, and how cardio and strength differ.

steps.title: The guidelines
steps.body:
U.S. Physical Activity Guidelines:

**Ages 6-17**: at least **60 minutes a day** of moderate-to-vigorous activity, with vigorous activity, muscle strengthening and bone strengthening (running, jumping) each at least **3 days a week**.

**Adults**: at least **150 minutes a week** of moderate activity (or **75 minutes** of vigorous), plus **muscle strengthening on 2 or more days**.

> Moderate: you can talk but not sing. Vigorous: you can only say a few words before catching your breath.
steps.tip: Try the talk test on your next walk or bike ride: if you can talk but not sing, it counts as moderate activity.

steps.prompt: An adult wants to hit 150 minutes of moderate activity over 5 days. How many minutes a day is that?
steps.explain: 150 / 5 = **30 minutes** a day, like a brisk 15-minute walk to and from school or work.
steps.hint: Split the weekly total evenly across the days. Divide.

steps.prompt: For adults, 1 minute of vigorous activity (like running hard) counts about the same as 2 minutes of moderate activity (like brisk walking).
steps.explain: That's why the adult guideline is 150 minutes of moderate **or** 75 minutes of vigorous activity a week. Mixing both is fine: two hard 20-minute runs count like 80 moderate minutes.

steps.title: Cardio vs strength
steps.body:
**Cardio (aerobic)**: running, biking, swimming, brisk walking, sports. Strengthens your heart and lungs, helps endurance and mood.

**Strength (muscle-strengthening)**: weights, bodyweight moves like push-ups and squats, resistance bands. Builds muscle and bone, protects joints, and makes everyday tasks easier.

You need both. Any activity beats none, and even short bouts add up.

source.label: CDC: Activity guidelines for children and teens

steps.tip: Pick two days this week for 20 minutes of bodyweight strength: squats, push-ups (on your knees or against a counter is fine) and a plank. Put them in your calendar.

steps.prompt: Match each activity to its main type.
steps.explain: Many activities count for more than one type. Jumping and running load your bones, which helps keep them strong.

steps.prompt: During a bike ride you can talk in full sentences but couldn't sing a song. What intensity is that?
options: Light
Moderate
Vigorous
Maximum
steps.explain: The talk test: talking but not singing is moderate. If you could only say a few words at a time, it's vigorous.
steps.hint: Use the talk test: talking is fine, but singing isn't possible.

steps.prompt: A 20-year-old works full time and says, 'I don't have an hour a day to exercise, so why bother?' What's the best advice?

options.text: Aim for 150 minutes a week in chunks that fit, like 30 minutes on 5 days, plus two short strength sessions.
options.feedback: Right. The adult target is weekly, and short bouts count.

options.text: Skip it until you have time for 2-hour gym sessions.
options.feedback: All-or-nothing thinking means nothing. Shorter sessions work.

options.text: Only do cardio; strength training is just for bodybuilders.
options.feedback: Adults are advised to do strength training at least 2 days a week for muscles, bones and joints.

steps.explain: Walking or biking for transport, taking stairs and quick home workouts all count toward the weekly goal.
steps.hint: Is the adult goal daily or weekly? Do short sessions count?

steps.prompt: Teens are advised to get at least 60 minutes of activity every day, not just 150 minutes a week.
steps.explain: Ages 6-17 have a daily target of 60 minutes. The 150-minute weekly target is for adults.

steps.prompt: Add up your activity over the last week. Where could you fit 2-3 more sessions, and which would be strength?

levels.title: Your Beginner Routine
levels.summary: Warm-ups, core strength moves, sets and reps, and progressive overload.

steps.title: Keep it simple
steps.body:
A good beginner plan is 2-3 full-body strength sessions a week on non-back-to-back days. Each one:

1. **Warm up** 5-10 minutes: light cardio plus moves like leg swings and arm circles.
2. **Main moves**, one from each pattern:
   - **Squat** (bodyweight or goblet squat)
   - **Hinge** (hip bridge, Romanian deadlift)
   - **Push** (push-ups, bench or dumbbell press)
   - **Pull** (rows, band pull-aparts)
   - **Core** (plank)
3. **Cool down** with easy walking and stretching.

Learn form first with light weight. Good form beats heavy weight.
steps.tip: Film one set of squats on your phone from the side. Check that your heels stay down and your back stays straight before you add any weight.

steps.prompt: Put a strength workout in order.
items: 5-10 minute warm-up
A lighter practice set of the first exercise
Working sets of squats, push-ups and rows
A core exercise like a plank
Cool-down walk and stretching
steps.explain: Warm-ups raise muscle temperature and rehearse the movement, which lowers injury risk.
steps.hint: Warm-up first, the hardest work in the middle, recovery at the end.

steps.title: Sets and reps
steps.body:
- A **rep** is one movement, like one squat.
- A **set** is a group of reps done in a row.
- "3 x 10" means 3 sets of 10 reps.

Rest 1-2 minutes between sets. End each set with about 1-3 reps left "in the tank", not at total failure.

Rest days matter too. Muscles rebuild between sessions, fueled by sleep and protein.
steps.tip: Log every workout in your phone notes: exercise, weight, and sets x reps. Seeing last week's numbers tells you exactly what to try today.

steps.prompt: You do 3 sets of 12 reps of bodyweight squats. How many squats is that in total?
steps.explain: 3 sets x 12 reps = **36 squats**. That's a solid beginner amount for one exercise.
steps.hint: 3 x 12 means 3 sets of 12 reps. Multiply.

steps.title: Progressive overload
steps.body:
Muscles get stronger when you slowly ask more of them. This is called **progressive overload**.

When a workout feels easy and your form is solid, add a little next time:
- one more rep, or
- one more set, or
- a small amount of weight (often 2.5-5 lb)

If your form breaks down, go back to the last weight. Slow and steady wins.
steps.tip: When you can finish every set with good form and 2-3 reps to spare, add one rep per set or the smallest weight jump next session.

steps.prompt: You've done goblet squats with a 25 lb dumbbell for 3 sets of 10. This week they felt easy and your form stayed solid. What's the best next step?
options: Add a little: try 30 lb, or do 12 reps per set
Jump to 50 lb to see results faster
Stay at 25 lb for 10 reps forever, since it's working
Do as many reps as you can until your legs give out
feedback: Right. A small step up keeps you progressing safely.
Big jumps usually wreck form and invite injury.
Without more challenge, progress stalls.
Going to total failure every time makes recovery harder and form sloppy.
steps.hint: Progressive overload means a small step up, not a giant leap.
steps.explain: Add one small thing at a time: a few pounds, a couple of reps, or one more set. Real progress isn't always steady; some weeks you'll repeat a weight, and that's fine.

steps.prompt: Match each term to its meaning.
pairs: A group of reps done in a row
Gradually increasing the challenge over time
Time for muscles to repair and grow
steps.explain: With these four ideas you can read and follow almost any training plan.

steps.prompt: You feel sharp pain in your shoulder during a bench press, not just muscle burn. What do you do?

options.text: Stop the exercise, rest it, and see a doctor or physical therapist if the pain continues.
options.feedback: Correct. Sharp or joint pain is a stop sign, unlike normal muscle burn.

options.text: Push through: no pain, no gain.
options.feedback: Pushing through sharp pain can turn a minor strain into a serious injury.

options.text: Add more weight to strengthen it.
options.feedback: Loading an injured joint makes it worse.

steps.explain: Muscle burn and next-day soreness are normal. Sharp, stabbing, or joint pain is not.
steps.hint: Is it normal muscle burn, or sharp pain in a joint?

steps.prompt: Beginners should add as much weight as possible each session to see results faster.
steps.explain: Small, steady increases with good form build strength and avoid injury. Big jumps usually lead to bad form or pain.

steps.title: Key takeaways
steps.body:
- 2-3 full-body sessions a week: squat, hinge, push, pull, core.
- Warm up first; learn form with light weight.
- Progressive overload: a little more each week.
- Muscle burn is normal; sharp pain means stop.
- Rest, sleep and protein are when you actually get stronger.

levels.title: Stress and Mood
levels.summary: What stress does, healthy ways to cope, and signs that it's more than stress.

steps.title: What stress is
steps.body:
Stress is your body's alarm system. Facing a test, a deadline or a conflict, your heart speeds up and your muscles tense so you can act. Short-term, that helps you perform.

When stress doesn't let up, it can show up as:
- trouble sleeping, or sleeping a lot
- headaches, stomachaches, tight shoulders
- irritability or snapping at people
- trouble concentrating
- eating much more or less than usual
steps.tip: Write down your top two body signs of stress, like a tight jaw or a stomachache. Spotting them early lets you step in before stress piles up.

steps.title: Tools that work
steps.body:
- **Move**: even a 10-minute walk lowers tension.
- **Sleep**: stress and short sleep feed each other.
- **Breathe slowly**: try breathing in for 4 counts and out for 6, for a few minutes.
- **Break it down**: write the problem down and pick the next small step.
- **Talk to someone** you trust.
- **Limit** doomscrolling, caffeine and alcohol or drugs, which make stress and sleep worse.

> Coping well isn't about never feeling stressed. It's about having healthy ways to come back down.
steps.tip: Try one minute of slow breathing right now: in for 4 counts, out for 6. Use it before your next test or hard conversation.

steps.prompt: Which are healthy ways to handle stress? Select all that apply.
options: Going for a walk or run
Writing a to-do list and starting the first small step
Using alcohol to fall asleep
Talking to a friend, parent or counselor
Scrolling social media until 2 a.m.
steps.explain: Movement, planning and talking help. Alcohol worsens sleep quality and mood, and late scrolling cuts into sleep.

steps.prompt: Put a 'stuck and overwhelmed' reset in order.
items: Pause and take five slow breaths
Write down everything that's on your mind
Circle the one task that matters most today
Break it into a first step you can do in 10 minutes
Do that step, then decide the next one
steps.explain: Overwhelm usually comes from holding everything in your head at once. Getting it on paper and shrinking the first step breaks the freeze.
steps.hint: Calm down first, then get everything out of your head, then shrink the first task.

steps.title: When it's more than stress
steps.body:
Everyone has bad days. It may be **depression** when, for **at least 2 weeks**, most of the day and nearly every day, you feel sad, empty or hopeless, or lose interest in things you used to enjoy, along with changes in sleep, appetite, energy or focus, or feelings of worthlessness.

**Anxiety** may be a disorder when worry is hard to control, happens most days, and comes with restlessness, tension, trouble sleeping or concentrating.

Both are common and **treatable**: therapy, lifestyle changes and sometimes medicine work.
steps.tip: If low mood or worry has lasted two weeks or more, book a visit with your doctor or school counselor this week. You can start with: "I haven't felt like myself for a while."

steps.prompt: For the past three weeks, your brother has skipped meals, quit basketball, which he loved, and barely leaves his room. He says he's 'just tired.' What's the best first step?

options.text: Talk to him privately, say what you've noticed without judging, listen, and encourage him to see a doctor or counselor. Tell a trusted adult if you're worried.
options.feedback: Yes. These changes have lasted more than two weeks, and caring, direct concern opens the door to help.

options.text: Leave him alone; he'll snap out of it.
options.feedback: Depression usually doesn't go away on its own, and isolation can deepen it.

options.text: Tell him to cheer up and stop being lazy.
options.feedback: This makes people feel misunderstood and less likely to open up.

steps.explain: Losing interest in things he loved, appetite changes and withdrawal for weeks are warning signs worth acting on.
steps.hint: How long has this lasted, and what has changed from how he used to be?

steps.prompt: Depression is a sign of weakness that people can fix by trying harder.
steps.explain: Depression is a common health condition, not a character flaw. It's treatable, and getting help is a strong move.

steps.prompt: What are your early signs that stress is building up, and which two tools from this lesson will you use next time?

units.title: Getting Help and First Aid
units.description: Reach mental health support, recognize emergencies and give basic first aid until help arrives.

levels.title: Getting Mental Health Help
levels.summary: Who to contact, the 988 Lifeline, and how to help a friend in crisis.

steps.title: Where to start
steps.body:
You don't have to be in crisis to ask for help.
- **A trusted adult**: parent, coach, teacher.
- **School or college counselor**: usually free.
- **Your primary care doctor**: can check for physical causes and refer you to a therapist.
- **Therapists**: your health insurance website lists in-network ones; many offer video visits.
- **Employee assistance programs (EAP)** at many jobs offer a few free counseling sessions.

It can take a couple of tries to find a therapist who's a good fit. That's normal.
steps.tip: Search your insurance website for in-network therapists who offer video visits, and save two names before you ever need them.

steps.title: 988: the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline
steps.body:
**Call or text 988**, or chat at the Lifeline's website, any time, day or night, for free, confidential support from a trained counselor. It's for anyone in emotional distress, thinking about suicide, struggling with substance use, or worried about someone else.

> If someone is in **immediate danger** (has a weapon, has taken pills, or is about to act), **call 911**.
steps.tip: Save 988 in your phone contacts now as "988 Crisis Line", so it's one tap away for you or a friend.

steps.prompt: Your friend texts late at night that they feel hopeless and don't see the point anymore. They're home and not in immediate danger. Which resource is built for this?
options: 988, by call or text
Their doctor's office voicemail
A public social media post asking for advice
Waiting to talk at school next week
steps.explain: 988 is answered 24/7 by trained crisis counselors, and you can contact it on a friend's behalf too. If they're in immediate danger, call 911.
steps.hint: Which option reaches a trained person tonight?

steps.title: Helping a friend
steps.body:
If you're worried about someone:
- **Ask directly**: "Are you thinking about killing yourself?" Asking does *not* put the idea in their head; it shows you care and can handle the answer.
- **Listen** without judging or rushing to fix.
- **Keep them safe**: if they have a plan or means, stay with them and get help.
- **Connect** them to 988, a counselor or a trusted adult.
- **Follow up** in the next days.

Never promise to keep suicide plans secret.
steps.tip: Say the direct question out loud once, alone: "Are you thinking about killing yourself?" It's much easier to ask in a real moment if you've practiced the words.

steps.prompt: Put the steps for helping a friend who might be thinking about suicide in order.
items: Ask them directly if they're thinking about suicide
Listen calmly without judging
Help keep them safe and away from anything they could use to hurt themselves
Connect them with 988 or a trusted adult
Check in with them again over the next days
steps.explain: Ask, listen, keep safe, connect, follow up. If danger is immediate, call 911 first.
steps.hint: Ask, listen, keep safe, connect, follow up.

steps.prompt: Asking someone directly whether they're thinking about suicide can put the idea in their head.
steps.explain: Research shows asking directly does not increase risk. It often brings relief and opens a conversation.

steps.prompt: A friend tells you about suicidal thoughts and makes you promise not to tell anyone. What should you do?

options.text: Tell them you care too much to keep it secret, and involve a trusted adult or 988, with them if possible.
options.feedback: Right. Their safety comes before the promise.

options.text: Keep the promise so they keep trusting you.
options.feedback: This leaves you alone with a life-or-death situation. Get help.

options.text: Post about it so other friends can help.
options.feedback: Public posts can embarrass them and don't bring trained help.

steps.explain: You can be a good friend and still get help. They may be upset at first; many people are later grateful.
steps.hint: Which matters more here: keeping a promise, or keeping your friend safe?

steps.prompt: Match the situation to the best resource.
pairs: Someone has taken pills and is hard to wake
You feel overwhelmed and need to talk tonight
Ongoing anxiety affecting school or work
Free short-term counseling through your job
steps.explain: Emergencies go to 911, crises to 988, and ongoing struggles to a professional who can work with you over time.

steps.prompt: Write down two people you could talk to if you were struggling, and save 988 in your phone's contacts.

levels.title: Emergencies, 911 and CPR
levels.summary: When to call 911, hands-only CPR and using an AED.

steps.title: Read this first
steps.body:
> These lessons are an introduction, **not a substitute for a certified CPR and first aid class**. Classes from the American Red Cross or American Heart Association take a few hours, include hands-on practice, and are often free or low-cost through schools and workplaces.

**Call 911** for:
- unresponsive, or not breathing normally
- chest pain or pressure; trouble breathing
- severe bleeding that won't stop
- signs of stroke: face drooping, arm weakness, slurred speech
- choking that doesn't clear
- seizures, serious burns, suspected overdose or poisoning
steps.tip: Save Poison Help, 1-800-222-1222, in your phone contacts. It's free and answered 24/7 for any possible poisoning. If the person collapses, has a seizure or can't breathe, call 911 instead.

steps.prompt: Which situations call for 911 right away? Select all that apply.
options: A coworker suddenly has a drooping face and slurred speech
A friend has a small paper cut
Someone collapses and isn't breathing normally
Your dad has crushing chest pain and is sweating
You have a mild sore throat
steps.explain: Stroke signs, collapse with abnormal breathing and chest pain are emergencies where minutes matter. Minor cuts and sore throats aren't.

steps.title: Hands-only CPR
steps.body:
If a teen or adult suddenly collapses and isn't breathing normally (or is only gasping):
1. Make sure the scene is safe.
2. Tap and shout. No response? **Call 911** on speaker and send someone for an **AED**.
3. **Push hard and fast** in the center of the chest: **100-120 pushes a minute**, at least **2 inches** deep but not more than 2.4 inches, letting the chest rise fully each time.
4. Keep going until an AED or trained help takes over.

For infants, children, drowning and overdose, rescue breaths are also important; a class teaches you how.

source.label: American Heart Association: What is CPR?

steps.tip: Sign up for a certified CPR and AED class from the American Red Cross or American Heart Association. Many schools and workplaces offer them free or at low cost.

steps.prompt: Someone collapses at a basketball game. Put the hands-only CPR steps in order.
items: Check that the scene is safe
Tap their shoulder and shout to check if they respond
Call 911 on speaker and send someone to get an AED
Start hard, fast chest compressions in the center of the chest
Use the AED as soon as it arrives and follow its voice prompts
steps.explain: Safety, check, call, compress, shock. Don't stop compressions to wait for help.
steps.hint: Safety, check, call, compress, shock.

steps.prompt: If another person can do CPR, it's smart to switch who does compressions about every 2 minutes.
steps.explain: Compressions get weaker as you tire, often without you noticing. At 100-120 a minute, 2 minutes is over 200 pushes. Swap fast so the pause is only a few seconds.

steps.title: AEDs: anyone can use one
steps.body:
An **automated external defibrillator (AED)** checks the heart's rhythm and, if needed, delivers a shock that can restart a normal beat. They're in schools, gyms, airports and offices.

- Turn it on: it **talks you through every step**.
- Put the pads on the bare chest as shown in the pictures.
- Make sure no one touches the person when it analyzes or shocks.
- Restart compressions right after a shock or if no shock is advised.

An AED won't shock someone who doesn't need it.
steps.tip: Next time you're at school, the gym or work, look for the AED sign and notice exactly where it is. Knowing ahead saves precious seconds.

steps.prompt: What compression rate does the American Heart Association recommend for CPR?
options: 40-60 per minute
60-80 per minute
100-120 per minute
150-180 per minute
steps.explain: 100-120 per minute, about the beat of the song 'Stayin' Alive.' Too slow doesn't move enough blood; too fast doesn't let the heart refill.
steps.hint: Think of a song with a fast, steady beat, faster than one beat per second.

steps.prompt: A man collapses at the gym and isn't breathing normally. Someone shouts that there's an AED by the front desk. You're the only other person nearby who's free. What do you do first?

options.text: Call 911 on speaker, ask the person at the front desk to bring the AED, and start compressions.
options.feedback: Correct. Getting 911, the AED and compressions going at once gives him the best chance.

options.text: Wait for paramedics so you don't do something wrong.
options.feedback: Every minute without CPR lowers survival. Good Samaritan laws generally protect people who help in good faith.

options.text: Check his pulse for a full minute before doing anything.
options.feedback: Long pulse checks waste critical time. If he's not breathing normally, start CPR.

steps.explain: Hands-only CPR and an AED, started fast, can double or triple survival from cardiac arrest.
steps.hint: Can you get several things moving at the same time?

steps.prompt: You need a CPR certification to legally use an AED in a public place.
steps.explain: AEDs are designed for untrained bystanders and talk you through each step. A class still builds confidence.

steps.title: Key takeaways
steps.body:
- Not breathing normally? Call 911, get an AED, push hard and fast.
- 100-120 compressions a minute, at least 2 inches deep.
- Turn on the AED and follow its voice prompts.
- Take a certified CPR class; these lessons aren't a substitute.

levels.title: Choking, Bleeding and Burns
levels.summary: First aid for the most common emergencies until help arrives.

steps.title: Choking
steps.body:
If someone can still **cough or talk**, encourage them to keep coughing.

If they **can't cough, talk or breathe** (often clutching their throat):
1. Have someone call 911.
2. Give **5 back blows** between the shoulder blades with the heel of your hand.
3. Give **5 abdominal thrusts** (fist just above the belly button, quick inward-upward pulls).
4. **Alternate** 5 and 5 until the object comes out or they become unresponsive.

If they become unresponsive, start CPR. For infants, use back blows and chest thrusts, never abdominal thrusts. These steps follow the AHA's 2025 guidelines.
steps.tip: Find the spot for abdominal thrusts on yourself: make a fist and place it just above your belly button, below the ribs. Knowing the spot helps you act fast.

steps.prompt: An adult at dinner is clutching their throat and can't speak or cough. Put the steps in order.
items: Ask 'Are you choking?' and have someone call 911
Give 5 firm back blows between the shoulder blades
Give 5 abdominal thrusts
Keep alternating back blows and abdominal thrusts
If they become unresponsive, start CPR
steps.explain: Cycles of 5 back blows and 5 abdominal thrusts, per the 2025 AHA guidelines, until the airway clears or CPR is needed.
steps.hint: Get help coming first. Back blows come before abdominal thrusts.

steps.title: Severe bleeding
steps.body:
1. **Call 911** for heavy bleeding, bleeding that won't stop, or signs of shock (pale, clammy skin, confusion, dizziness).
2. Put on gloves if you have them.
3. **Press firmly and directly** on the wound with a clean cloth or bandage, and keep pressing.
4. **Don't lift it to check.** If blood soaks through, add more layers on top.
5. For life-threatening limb bleeding that pressure doesn't stop, a **tourniquet** goes 2-3 inches above the wound (not on a joint). Note the time you applied it.
steps.tip: Keep a basic first aid kit at home and in the car, with gloves, gauze pads and a roll of bandage. Check it twice a year and restock what you used.

steps.prompt: You're pressing a towel on a deep cut and blood soaks through. What do you do?
options: Remove the towel and replace it with a fresh one
Add another cloth on top and keep pressing
Lift it every minute to check the wound
Rinse the wound under the faucet to see how deep it is
steps.explain: Removing a soaked dressing can pull away clots that are forming. Add layers and keep firm pressure.
steps.hint: Lifting or removing the cloth can pull away the clot that's forming.

steps.title: Burns
steps.body:
For a minor heat burn:
- **Cool it under cool (not ice-cold) running water**, ideally for 10-20 minutes. Different groups give slightly different times; the key is starting fast and cooling for several minutes.
- Remove rings, watches or tight clothing near the burn before it swells.
- Cover loosely with a clean, nonstick dressing.
- **Don't** use ice, butter, oils or toothpaste, and don't pop blisters.

**Get emergency care** for large or deep burns; burns on the face, hands, feet, genitals or major joints; chemical or electrical burns; or any burn with trouble breathing.
steps.tip: Tell everyone you live with the burn rule: cool running water, never ice or butter. Tape a note inside a kitchen cabinet so it's there when you need it.

steps.prompt: You grab a hot pan handle and get a small red burn on your palm. Which are correct first aid steps? Select all that apply.
options: Run cool water over it for several minutes
Rub butter on it
Take off your ring before your hand swells
Hold an ice cube on it
Cover it loosely with a clean, nonstick bandage
steps.explain: Cool water, removing jewelry and a loose clean cover help. Butter traps heat and ice can damage skin further.

steps.prompt: Match each emergency to the key first aid action.
pairs: Alternate 5 back blows and 5 abdominal thrusts
Firm, direct pressure; tourniquet if it won't stop
steps.explain: In every case, call or have someone call 911 when it's serious, and keep helping until trained responders take over.

steps.prompt: Your friend spilled boiling water down their leg. The burn covers a large part of the thigh and is blistering badly. What's the best response?

options.text: Call 911 or get them to emergency care, and cool the burn with cool running water while you wait.
options.feedback: Correct. Large, blistering burns need professional care. Cooling starts treatment now.

options.text: Pop the blisters so it heals faster.
options.feedback: Blisters protect against infection. Don't pop them.

options.text: Pack it in ice to stop the pain.
options.feedback: Ice on a large burn can damage tissue and drop body temperature.

steps.explain: Large or deep burns, or burns on the face, hands, feet, genitals or joints, need emergency care.
steps.hint: Is this a small burn, or one that needs professional care?

steps.title: Key takeaways
steps.body:
- Choking: alternate 5 back blows and 5 abdominal thrusts; CPR if they become unresponsive.
- Bleeding: firm direct pressure, add layers, tourniquet for life-threatening limb bleeding.
- Burns: cool running water, no ice or butter, cover loosely.
- Call 911 when it's serious.
- Take a certified first aid and CPR class; practice is what makes it stick.
